Tatnai
TAT-nye
proper noun
Aramaic Tattenay (H8674), a Persian name of uncertain meaning, commonly read as gift; the title that follows it, governor on this side the river, is the satrapal office over the province Beyond the River.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tatnai was the Persian governor of the province Beyond the River in the reign of Darius, and he is the rarest kind of figure in Scripture: an unbelieving official who does his job honestly and thereby serves the purposes of God. When the elders of the Jews resumed building the temple, Tatnai came and asked the obvious question of any provincial governor — Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall? (Ezr 5:3). He did not stop the work. He took down the names, listened to the Jews' answer that Cyrus had decreed it, and wrote to Darius asking that the royal archives be searched (Ezr 5:6). The search found the decree at Achmetha, and Darius not only confirmed it but ordered Tatnai to fund the work out of the king's tribute and supply the sacrifices. Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river… according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily (Ezr 6:13). Ezra gives the reason the inquiry did not become a stoppage: the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease (Ezr 5:5).

Origin & Era

Persian governor of the province Beyond the River under Darius, who questioned the rebuilding of the temple but referred the matter honestly to the king.

expand to see more

TATNAI, Aramaic Tattenay, a Persian name, commonly read gift.

Governor on this side the river in the reign of Darius king of Persia.

He questioned the Jews concerning their authority to rebuild the house of God.

He wrote to Darius asking that the decree of Cyrus be searched for in the archives.

When Darius confirmed the decree, he executed it speedily.

Key Scripture

Ezr 5:3 — "At the same time came to them Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and their companions, and said thus unto them, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?"

Ezr 5:6 — "The copy of the letter that Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and his companions the Apharsachites, which were on this side the river, sent unto Darius the king:"

Ezr 6:13 — "Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river, Shetharboznai, and their companions, according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily."

Ezr 5:5 — "But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease, till the matter came to Darius: and then they returned answer by letter concerning this matter."

Modern Corruption

Civil authority is cast as either sacred or hostile; Scripture shows an unconverted magistrate doing justice and thereby serving God's ends.

expand to see more

Christians commonly hold one of two unbalanced views of the magistrate. The first baptises the state, treating political power as the church's natural ally and its favour as evidence of God's blessing. The second treats every civil authority as an enemy in waiting, so that any inquiry from an official is read as persecution beginning. Tatnai fits neither. He was a pagan officer of a pagan empire, he asked a searching question about a Jewish building project, and he asked it properly — through the archives and the courts rather than by force, which is exactly what Rehum and Shimshai had refused to do a chapter earlier.

Scripture's settled doctrine is that the magistrate is God's minister for good, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil (Rom 13:4), whether or not he knows whose servant he is. Cyrus is called the LORD's anointed and the LORD says of him I girded thee, though thou hast not known me (Isa 45:5). The principle to recover is that honest procedure in the hands of an unbeliever is a real mercy from God, worth honouring and worth praying for — for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life (1Ti 2:2).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic Tattenay (H8674), a Persian personal name; the office is pechah (H6347), a governor of a province.

expand to see more

Aramaic Tattenay (H8674) — Tatnai, governor beyond the river; Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6, 6:13.

Aramaic pechah (H6347) — a governor, a satrap's deputy; the office held by Tatnai and later by Nehemiah in Judah.

Aramaic abar naharah — Beyond the River, the Persian province west of the Euphrates containing Judah.

Hebrew ayin (H5869) — an eye; the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews (Ezr 5:5).

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a minister, a servant; he is the minister of God to thee for good (Rom 13:4).

Usage

"“Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?”"

"“According to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily”."
